issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may reappraise evidence only where the factual findings below are perverse or otherwise disclose a substantial question of law.
material_facts: The matter reached the High Court in a second appeal after the first appellate court reversed the trial court’s finding that the landlord had a bona fide need for the premises.

The first appellate court inferred that the need was a pretext to increase rent, although rent had not been increased for several years and there had been no pleaded attempt to increase it during that period.
The High Court found the first appellate court’s conclusion erroneous, and the Supreme Court agreed that it was perverse.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to entertain the second appeal and reappraise the evidence because the first appellate court’s finding was perverse.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal ordinarily lies only on a substantial question of law, not merely because a factual finding is disputed. A finding based on no evidence, irrelevant material, misreading of evidence, or an erroneous approach may be perverse and raise a substantial question of law warranting reappraisal. The Court relied on Ram Prasad Rajak v. Nand Kumar & Bros., Reserve Bank of India v. Ramakrishna Govind Morey, Kulwant Kaur v. Gurdial Singh Mann, Rajappa Hanamantha Ranoji v. Mahadev Channabasappa, Jai Singh v. Shakuntala, P. Chandrasekharan v. S. Kanakarajan, and Jagdish Singh v. Nathu Singh.

predicates.second_appeal: The matter is an appeal from a decision made in a second appeal.
predicates.lower_finding_perverse: A lower court’s factual finding rests on no evidence, irrelevant material, misread evidence, or an erroneous approach.

issues.definition: When a matter is a second appeal and the lower factual finding is perverse, reappraisal by the second appellate court is permitted.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s need to use tenanted premises for the landlord’s own business is bona fide when it is a genuine need rather than a pretext for evicting the tenant.
material_facts: The landlord conducted a business from a rented space measuring 3 feet by 4 feet on a platform over a drain, on land occupied by encroachment, while the tenanted shop measured 18 feet by 14 feet and was situated on a main road in a market.
The landlord wanted to conduct the business from the tenanted shop; the landlord’s son was working abroad and had not testified that he intended to join the business.
The rent had been increased over time, but it had not been increased since 1995, and there was no pleading of an attempt to increase it during the seven years before the eviction suit.
The landlord’s failure to occupy the shop after an earlier tenant vacated it had occurred many years before the suit.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s need was bona fide; the earlier rent increases, the son’s employment abroad, and the remote failure to occupy the premises did not establish that the need was a pretext.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(1)(f) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 permits eviction for the landlord’s bona fide requirement. The landlord is generally the best judge of the landlord’s requirement and courts should not dictate how the landlord conducts business, but the need must be real, genuine, and in good faith rather than fanciful or a ruse. The circumstances relevant to need are assessed as they exist when the suit is instituted, and remote events may not be relevant. The Court relied on Prativa Devi v. T.V. Krishnan, Ram Dass v. Ishwar Chander, Rahabhar Productions Pvt. Ltd. v. Rajendra K. Tandon, Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Dr. Mahesh Chand Gupta, Malpe Vishwanath Acharya v. State of Maharashtra, and Siddalingamma v. Mamtha Shenoy.

rule.if: eviction_for_landlord_business_need and landlord_uses_inadequate_business_space and landlord_intends_to_use_tenanted_premises and no_current_rent_pressure_evidence

predicates.eviction_for_landlord_business_need: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground that the landlord needs the premises for the landlord’s business.
predicates.landlord_uses_inadequate_business_space: The landlord conducts business from space that is markedly inadequate or unsuitable.
predicates.landlord_intends_to_use_tenanted_premise: The landlord intends to conduct the landlord’s business in the tenanted premises.
predicates.no_current_rent_pressure_evidence: The evidence does not show a current attempt to use the asserted need as a pretext to increase rent.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding for the landlord’s business need, inadequate present business space, an intention to use the premises, and absence of evidence of current rent pressure support a finding of bona fide need.

issues.legal_issue: Where a landlord has a bona fide need for tenanted premises, partial eviction may be ordered when the premises can be divided and partial possession can accommodate the competing interests.
material_facts: The shop measured 18 feet by 14 feet, and the landlord’s existing business space measured only 3 feet by 4 feet.
The High Court had not considered the magnitude of the landlord’s business or whether partial eviction could serve the purpose of both landlord and tenant.
The Supreme Court directed that possession be recovered of half the premises, divided on either side.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was allowed in part, and the landlord was awarded possession of half the premises.
issues.legal_principle: In deciding the extent of eviction, the relevant considerations include the magnitude of the landlord’s business and whether partial eviction can serve the purpose of both parties. The Court applied these considerations to reach an equitable order in the circumstances of the case.

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant from premises.
predicates.bona_fide_need_established: The landlord has a genuine need to use the premises.
predicates.premises_can_be_divided: The premises can be divided so that possession of less than the whole can be transferred.

issues.definition: When a landlord has a genuine need in an eviction proceeding and the premises can be divided, partial possession may be ordered.
